sections.overview: The common pheasant is a large ground-dwelling bird native to temperate Asia, introduced elsewhere by people.
sections.identification: Adults have a compact body, strong legs and a long tapering tail; males are usually larger, often 75–90 cm long including the tail. The male is vividly coloured with a red face, green head and copper body; females are smaller and mottled brown, and the white neck ring is not universal. Cornell reports a combined-sex range of 50–70 cm in length, 500–3,000 g in mass and 56–86 cm in wingspan; males are usually larger and have much longer tails, but the guide does not separate its measurement ranges by sex.
sections.habitat: Its native range reaches from the Caucasus and western Asia through China, across open woodland, scrub and grassland with nearby dense cover. Introductions spread it through Europe and North America, where self-sustaining wild populations coexist with farmed birds and seasonal releases. It also uses field margins, hedges and grassy ditches for shelter beside feeding areas.
sections.diet: It scratches the ground for seeds, grains, roots and fallen fruit, adding leaves and buds; in spring and summer it takes more insects and other invertebrates. Newly hatched chicks rely especially on animal prey before their diet shifts toward more plant food over the following weeks.
sections.behavior: Breeding males announce and defend territories with loud calls, wing-drumming and spread-tail displays; one male may mate with several inconspicuous females. The species usually walks or runs, but when startled it launches almost vertically with rattling wingbeats, then flies a short distance to cover. Outside breeding, females may gather in flocks, with larger groups in winter than in summer.
sections.reproduction: The female lays about 7–15 eggs in a shallow ground nest and alone incubates them for roughly 23–28 days; downy chicks leave soon after hatching, feed themselves, follow her, and can make short flights at about two weeks.
sections.ecology: Pheasants forage along field margins, while foxes and other predators take eggs and chicks. Introduced birds can compete with native gamebirds for food and nesting space, so local effects vary with habitat and release density.
sections.conservation: The global IUCN assessment published in 2016 classified it as Least Concern but reported a decreasing trend. That assessment estimated 160–220 million mature birds worldwide, despite declines in parts of its range.
